title: Idempotent Eikonal Ray Marching: Curvature-Bounded Contraction and Fixed-Point Projection for Real-Time Implicit Surface Rendering
abstract: Rendering implicit surfaces, neural signed distance fields (SDFs), and level sets on resource-constrained mobile and XR platforms is fundamentally hindered by the computational stall of sphere tracing near grazing angles and silhouette edges. In standard sphere tracing, the spatial advance is conservatively bounded by the radial distance φ(r(t)), which approaches zero near surface horizons even when the ray intersects geometry far along its directional path. This induces severe iteration inflation (40–60+ steps per ray) and tail-latency spikes. In this paper, we formulate ray-surface intersection as a curvature-accelerated contraction operator Phit on the Eikonal distance field. By evaluating directional first- and second-order derivatives along the one-dimensional ray trajectory, Phit constructs a rational Halley contraction bounded by dynamic Lipschitz safety constraints. To balance arithmetic throughput against query evaluation complexity, we introduce an Adaptive Hybrid Marcher that executes single-query Lipschitz advances in open space and selectively activates second-order Halley contraction only within grazing silhouette horizons. Upon entering the root neighborhood, the operator achieves terminal orthogonal projection with fixed-point invariance (||Phit2 - Phit|| ≤ 10−15). We implement the engine in C++20 with AVX2 acceleration, thread-safe re-entrant context encapsulation, and zero dynamic heap allocation during traversal. Empirical benchmarks across constructive solid geometry (CSG) manifolds and authentic 3D biological cortical meshes demonstrate throughput of 27.0–33.3 MRays/s on multi-threaded CPUs. While classical sphere tracing retains higher raw throughput on simple analytical primitives due to single-query simplicity, our adaptive hybrid formulation truncates the grazing stall tail by up to 4× on silhouette rays (reducing traversal from 55 to 14 steps) with a 20% reduction in full-frame mean iterations (14.6 to 11.6 steps), providing deterministic frame pacing for latency-critical applications.
